common_name: Apricot Beauty Tulip (Salmon-Apricot Single Early Tulip)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall four to six inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil; Apricot Beauty is a long-standing Single Early division favorite valued for flowering well ahead of most other tulips.

directions: Plant bulbs four to six inches deep in full sun in fall, in soil that drains well over winter. Apricot Beauty belongs to the Single Early division and opens soft salmon-apricot blooms flushed with rose and a warm peachy glow that deepens as the flowers age, often with a light, pleasant fragrance. Its relatively short, sturdy stems make it a reliable choice for borders, containers, and forcing, and it is one of the most widely planted early-season tulips for its dependable performance. Lift and divide congested clumps every few years if blooms begin to decline in size.

common_name: Monte Carlo Tulip (Golden-Yellow Double Early Tulip)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall four to six inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil; Monte Carlo is a Double Early division tulip whose large, long-lasting blooms resemble a peony flower but open weeks earlier in the season.

directions: Plant bulbs four to six inches deep in full sun in fall, in soil that drains well over winter. Monte Carlo carries the Double Early division's hallmark fully double, bowl-shaped blooms in a rich buttery yellow, with a light fragrance and sturdy, wind-resistant stems shorter than most later tulip types. The multiple rows of broad petals give each flower a lasting, peony-like fullness that holds up unusually well in rain and wind compared with single-flowered tulips. Because the short stems resist lodging, it is a dependable choice for front-of-border plantings and mass bedding displays.

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall six to eight inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil; Daydream is a Darwin Hybrid division tulip whose large flowers shift color noticeably as they age through the bloom period.

directions: Plant bulbs six to eight inches deep in full sun in fall, in soil that drains well over winter. Daydream is a tall Darwin Hybrid tulip that opens soft buttery yellow and gradually deepens to warm apricot-orange as the large, egg-shaped blooms mature, giving a single planting two distinct color phases. Like other Darwin hybrids, it tends to perennialize better than many tulip types where winters provide adequate chill, and its sturdy stems hold up well to wind and rain. Plant it where the color transition can be appreciated up close, such as along a path or in a cutting bed.

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall four to six inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil; Toronto is a Greigii division tulip that typically produces two to three blooms per bulb on mottled, maroon-streaked foliage.

directions: Plant bulbs four to six inches deep in full sun in fall, in soil that drains well over winter. Toronto is an unusual multi-flowered Greigii tulip, with most bulbs sending up two to three coral-red blooms per stem above the division's characteristic low rosette of wavy, purple-mottled foliage. common_name: Horned Tulip (Fire Tulip, Spidery Red-and-Yellow Botanical Tulip)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall four to six inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil; the Horned Tulip has been cultivated for centuries and is of uncertain wild origin, grown today as a distinctive botanical curiosity in the Miscellaneous division.

directions: Plant bulbs four to six inches deep in full sun in fall, in soil that drains well over winter. The Horned Tulip bears narrow, twisting petals drawn out into slender, pointed tips, colored in streaks of fiery red and yellow that give the flower a wild, almost spidery look unlike any ordinary garden tulip. Long grown by collectors as a curiosity, its true wild origin has never been firmly established, and it persists in cultivation mainly through heirloom bulb specialists. Its slender form and unusual coloring make it a conversation-starting addition among rock garden plantings or other botanical species tulips.
